readme.title: What this module covers
readme.html:
What this module covers

This module looks past Amazon EC2 at the full spectrum of AWS compute, from unmanaged to managed to serverless. It covers AWS Lambda for event-driven code, containers with the AWS services that store, orchestrate and host them, and four purpose-built services for specific needs. The goal is to pick the service whose balance of control and convenience fits each workload.

readme.title: Lessons
readme.html:
Lessons

Module 3 Introduction

  1. Introduction to Serverless Computing: unmanaged, managed and serverless services, and who is responsible for what.

AWS Serverless, Containers, and Solutions Overview

  1. AWS Lambda: event-driven functions, triggers, runtimes, millisecond billing and the 15-minute limit.
  2. Containers and Orchestration on AWS: containers versus VMs, Amazon ECR, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS and AWS Fargate.
  3. Additional Compute Services: AWS Elastic Beanstalk, AWS Batch, Amazon Lightsail and AWS Outposts.

readme.title: Key takeaways
readme.html:
Key takeaways

  • Unmanaged EC2 leaves the OS and apps to you, managed services shift operations to AWS, and serverless hides servers entirely.
  • In serverless, AWS owns provisioning, scaling, availability and maintenance, while you own your code and its permissions.
  • Lambda runs code on triggers, scales automatically, bills per millisecond of compute and caps each run at 15 minutes.
  • Lambda is a poor fit for long jobs, for web servers that need OS-level control and for hosting databases.
  • Containers bundle an app with everything it needs, so it behaves the same in every environment and starts faster than a VM.
  • ECR stores images securely, ECS or EKS orchestrates them, and EC2 or Fargate is where they actually run.
  • Pick EKS when you want Kubernetes, which suits large or hybrid setups, and ECS when you want a streamlined, integrated orchestrator.
  • Fargate is the serverless way to host containers, while EC2 gives full control at the cost of managing instances.
  • Elastic Beanstalk deploys web apps for you, AWS Batch handles large parallel jobs, Lightsail offers cost-effective hosting at a predictable monthly price, and Outposts brings AWS on premises.

readme.title: What the assessment focuses on
readme.html:
What the assessment focuses on

The assessment has 8 questions.

  • Serverless service model and the customer's remaining responsibility (the code): 2 questions.
  • When AWS Lambda fits (short, event-driven work) and when it does not (long jobs, web servers needing OS control, databases): 1 question.
  • Lambda as a wrong option to rule out: 4 more questions.
  • Containers for making an app run the same in every environment: 1 question.
  • Container orchestration with Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS: 2 questions.
  • Amazon ECR as the secure image store: 1 question, with ECR also given as background in 1 more.
  • AWS Fargate for running containers without servers: 1 question.
  • AWS Batch for large, parallel, scheduled compute jobs: 1 question.
  • Amazon Lightsail for simple, low-traffic, cost-effective hosting: 1 question.
  • Amazon EC2 as the wrong choice when servers should not be managed or container orchestration is needed: 3 questions.
  • Other service models (unmanaged, on premises, hybrid cloud) as wrong choices next to serverless: 1 question.
  • Elastic Beanstalk, Lightsail, Fargate and AWS Batch as wrong choices in the AWS Batch and Lightsail questions: 2 questions.

readme.title: Summary
readme.html:
Summary

  • Picking compute is a trade between control and convenience: EC2 when you want to run everything yourself, fully managed Lambda or Fargate when you would rather not.
  • Containers fixed apps behaving differently from one environment to the next, and ECS and EKS take over the work of running and scaling them.
  • Four purpose-built services fill specific gaps: Lightsail for simple hosting, AWS Batch for big batch workloads, Elastic Beanstalk for web app deployment and Outposts for hybrid cloud.

introduction-to-serverless-computing.html:
Introduction to Serverless Computing

Objectives

  • Tell unmanaged, managed and serverless compute services apart.
  • State what AWS and the customer each own with serverless compute.

Notes

Roadmap

  • means AWS looks after the infrastructure under your app.
  • Next: , then , and for easier containers and deployment.

Amazon EC2: unmanaged

  • EC2 virtual machines suit anything from a basic web server to high performance computing.
  • You get fine control, but patching, scaling and the OS are yours while AWS runs the hardware.
  • Per the , AWS owns and you own .

Managed services

  • After you configure one, AWS keeps it running with no server management on your part.
  • , SNS and SQS are earlier examples.

Coffee shop analogy

  • Unmanaged is a high-end espresso machine: total control over beans, grind and knobs, plus all the upkeep.
  • Managed is a pod machine: pop in a pod and press a button, trading customization for speed.
  • Sometimes you want to play barista, and sometimes you just want fast coffee.

Serverless (fully managed)

  • Taking infrastructure management away entirely gave rise to serverless.
  • The servers hosting your app are hidden and out of reach.
  • AWS handles provisioning, maintenance, scaling and .

Picking a service

  • Each step toward managed trades control for convenience, so pick what your app needs.

Responsibility spectrum

  • Unmanaged, like EC2: AWS covers the physical layer, while each instance's OS, network setup and apps are yours to set up, secure and maintain.
  • Managed: AWS absorbs much of the operational overhead, though some provisioning or configuration may remain yours depending on the service.
  • Fully managed, like serverless Lambda: there are no servers for you to provision or manage, and AWS also covers scaling and availability.
  • What stays with you under Lambda is the application code and keeping it secure.
  • Later lessons also call Elastic Beanstalk, Batch, Outposts, ECS, EKS and ECR "fully managed", more loosely.

Visuals

  • Responsibility timeline (two steps): your share shrinks with managed services and shrinks again with fully managed (serverless) ones.

Key takeaways

  • The service model tells you which tasks are AWS's and which are yours.
  • With EC2, you configure, secure and maintain the OS, networking and apps on each instance.
  • Managed services cut infrastructure work, though some setup may remain.
  • Serverless leaves you only your code and its security.

Terms

  • Unmanaged service: a service such as EC2 where you handle the OS, patching and scaling.
  • Managed service: a service you configure while AWS runs it day to day.
  • Fully managed service: in this lesson's model, a service such as a serverless one where AWS runs every server and you look after just your code.
  • Serverless computing: running apps on servers you never see, which AWS provisions, scales and maintains.

aws-lambda.html:
AWS Lambda

Objectives

  • Recall what is and does as a serverless compute service.
  • Identify its parts: functions, triggers, runtimes and scaling.

Notes

What Lambda is

  • Lambda is a serverless compute service, also called .
  • Deploying an app like the narrator's crab classifier would otherwise mean provisioning, scaling and keeping servers available.
  • Instead, you deploy a function holding your code, and it runs whenever its fires.
  • Lambda plugs easily into other AWS services, so whole apps can run without managing servers.

Triggers

  • They range from simple events, like an upload or a finished classification, to heavier ones like a live data stream or resizing one image into several resolutions.

Scaling and limits

  • It is highly available and scales up or down by itself, from one trigger to thousands.
  • AWS patches, updates and secures the underlying environment and allocates its resources.
  • A run lasts 15 minutes at most, so work that cannot be split into such chunks may fit elsewhere.
  • Good fits are brief jobs kicked off by events, such as producing expense reports, crunching data in batches or serving web requests.

Runtimes

  • The course says Lambda supports any language: Java, Python and Node.js come built in, and you can build a .
  • Each is a go-between for one language: it hands your function the invocation event and context details, then returns the function's reply to Lambda.

How Lambda works

  1. Upload code, which becomes a function.
  2. Set an event source, such as an AWS service, mobile app or HTTP request.
  3. Code runs only on events, while Lambda handles servers and scaling.
  4. You pay for compute time only, per millisecond, priced by allocated memory.
  • Memory size is also how you tune performance.

Use cases

  • Three industry cases, in social media, news and gaming, show the same payoffs: a bill only for real usage, elastic scale and less ops work.

Demo: SQS triggers Lambda

  • Each new SQS message invokes a function built from an SQS .
  • An lets the function read the queue.
  • The queue emptied almost at once, and confirmed each message was processed.

Your share

  • You own the code and the roles and permissions the function uses to reach other services.

Visuals

  • How Lambda works: four markers from code upload to trigger, event-only execution and pay-per-use billing.
  • SQS demo architecture: a queue invoking a function per message, showing event-driven flow and the permissions it needs.

Key takeaways

  • Lambda runs code on events with no servers to manage.
  • Functions, triggers and runtimes are its core parts.
  • AWS handles automatic scaling, availability and patching.
  • You pay per millisecond of compute, priced by memory.
  • The 15-minute cap suits short, event-driven tasks.
  • You still own your code and its IAM permissions.

Scenarios

  • Crab classifier: photo uploads trigger classification and user alerts with no servers to run (functions and triggers).
  • Social media app: each upload is resized, filtered and stored, paying only for the processing time per image (event-driven Lambda).
  • News aggregator: articles are personalized when users open the app or search, scaling with traffic and saving cost by running only on interaction (pay-per-use).
  • Online game: thousands of real-time player events update scores and state, with costs tracking usage at peak times (real-time Lambda).

Terms

  • AWS Lambda: AWS's event-driven, serverless way to run code.
  • Function as a Service: Lambda's model of running your functions on demand.
  • Lambda function: the uploaded code Lambda runs when triggered.
  • Trigger: the event, such as an upload, queue message or HTTP request, that invokes a function.
  • Runtime: a per-language go-between that feeds a function its event and context data and passes the reply back to Lambda.
  • Custom runtime: a runtime you build yourself instead of a built-in one.
  • Blueprint: a ready-made function template with code and runtime preset.
  • Execution role: the IAM role granting a function access to other services.
  • CloudWatch Logs: the log groups and streams recording each run of a function.

containers-and-orchestration-on-aws.html:
Containers and Orchestration on AWS

Objectives

  • Explain how containers make an app's environment consistent and portable.
  • Explain how stores, manages and versions images.
  • Identify how ECS and EKS deploy, scale and manage containers.
  • Describe Fargate as serverless hosting for containers.

Notes

Why containers

  • "It works on my machine": apps run locally but fail elsewhere because environments differ.
  • A packs code, runtime, dependencies and configuration into one isolated unit that runs the same anywhere.
  • It is not a way to reach several operating systems, and it still needs configuration files.

Containers versus VMs

  • Containers share the host's OS, so they are lighter, start faster and use resources better.
  • A VM runs its own full OS on a , making it heavier and slower to start.

Why orchestration

  • Running containers yourself on EC2 means owning health checks, starts, stops, updates and networking.
  • That breaks down once a few containers on one host become thousands on many.
  • Containers do not scale themselves, so orchestrators run their lifecycle across a cluster, scale them with traffic, and handle recovery, monitoring and updates.

AWS container tools

  • AWS groups them as orchestration (ECS, EKS), registry (ECR) and compute (EC2, Fargate, where containers actually run).
  • In practice: push images to ECR, pick ECS or EKS, then pick EC2 or Fargate.

Orchestrators: ECS and EKS

  • ECS is the streamlined, integrated orchestrator, for containers and others.
  • You set images plus resources like instance types and load balancers, and ECS manages the rest.
  • EKS runs , the open source platform automating container deployment, scaling and management.
  • AWS fully manages EKS, while Kubernetes gets updates and support from its open source community.
  • EKS suits large-scale or hybrid setups that want extra control and flexibility.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, Amazon ECS The exam guide spells out Amazon Elastic Container Service (), the fully managed AWS service for orchestrating containers.
  • Exam guide update verified 2026-10-09, What is Amazon EKS? With Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (), AWS operates the Kubernetes control plane of each cluster for you.

Amazon ECR

  • A fully managed registry to keep, manage and deploy images, stored securely in repositories.
  • Orchestrators pull images from it, and you push and pull with standard tools and CLIs.
  • Images must meet standards.

Launch types for ECS and EKS: EC2 or Fargate

  • EC2: you manage the VMs under your containers, for full control plus upkeep.
  • Fargate: serverless, so AWS runs the servers while ECS or EKS orchestrates, and you pay only for resources used.

Visuals

  • Key takeaways timeline (three steps): containers versus VMs, consistent environments cutting failed deployments, and orchestration as containers multiply.

Key takeaways

  • Containers bundle an app and its dependencies into one portable unit, which suits workloads needing high security, reliability and scalability.
  • Sharing the host OS makes them lighter and faster than VMs.
  • ECS or EKS adds the scaling and lifecycle care that containers lack on their own.
  • Choose EKS for Kubernetes and large or hybrid setups, and ECS for a streamlined, integrated option.
  • ECR stores images securely, ECS or EKS orchestrates them, and EC2 or serverless Fargate runs them.

Scenarios

  • Small or medium business app needing specific hardware or networking: ECS on EC2.
  • Startup web app with variable traffic: ECS on Fargate.
  • Enterprise with complex, large workloads needing deep instance tuning: EKS on EC2.
  • Team wanting Kubernetes without managing servers: EKS on Fargate.

Terms

  • Container: a portable, isolated package of an app with all it needs to run.
  • Virtual machine (VM): a virtual computer with its own full OS.
  • Hypervisor: the layer letting each VM run its own full OS.
  • Container orchestration: automated lifecycle, scaling and health management for many containers.
  • Launch type: the compute, EC2 or Fargate, under ECS or EKS.
  • Amazon ECS: AWS's streamlined, integrated container orchestrator.
  • Amazon EKS: AWS's fully managed service for Kubernetes clusters.
  • Kubernetes: the open source container platform EKS runs.
  • Amazon ECR: AWS's fully managed container image registry.
  • AWS Fargate: serverless container hosting for ECS and EKS.
  • Docker: a platform for quickly building, testing and shipping apps.
  • Open Container Initiative (OCI): the image standards ECR supports.

additional-compute-services.html:
Additional Compute Services

Objectives

  • Explain how Elastic Beanstalk eases environment setup.
  • Explain how runs big jobs at scale.
  • Identify how Lightsail makes web hosting simple.
  • Describe how Outposts brings AWS on premises for .

Notes

AWS Elastic Beanstalk

  • Give this code and settings, and it builds the EC2 setup, scaling, load balancing and health checks.
  • You can save configurations to redeploy and still control every resource.
  • Raw EC2, by contrast, leaves deployment and scaling to you.
  • It supports Java, Python, Docker and more, for web apps, APIs and microservices.

AWS Batch

  • A fully managed service for heavy compute such as huge datasets, simulations and complex math.
  • It schedules jobs and scales resources to fit them across a fleet such as EC2 instances.
  • It fits parallel work like genomics, media transcoding and ML training.

Amazon Lightsail

  • A cost-effective bundle: virtual private servers (VPSs) plus storage, databases and networking, for a predictable monthly price.
  • It skips the complexity of traditional hosting and the full .
  • It fits blogs, small or low-traffic sites, and dev and test.

AWS Outposts

  • A fully managed hybrid cloud offering that brings AWS compute, storage and networking into your .
  • AWS services run locally with the same tools and APIs as in the cloud.
  • It fits compliance, data residency, low latency, remote sites and legacy app modernization.

Key takeaways

  • Each service is purpose-built, so match it to the job.
  • Elastic Beanstalk deploys, scales and monitors web apps you still control.
  • AWS Batch schedules and scales large parallel jobs.
  • Lightsail is the simple, predictably priced pick for small sites.
  • Outposts is the only one of the four on premises.

Terms

  • AWS Elastic Beanstalk: a service turning your code into a running, auto-scaled web environment.
  • AWS Batch: a service that plans and scales compute for batch jobs.
  • Batch computing: running large, compute-heavy jobs, often in parallel.
  • Amazon Lightsail: easy, budget-friendly AWS hosting for small sites.
  • Virtual private server (VPS): the server in Lightsail's monthly bundle.
  • AWS Outposts: AWS infrastructure running in your own data center.
  • Hybrid cloud: on-premises infrastructure used alongside AWS.

labs.brief: The cafe's menu export runs one short burst a week and its order worker runs all month; run each on AWS Lambda or an always-on Amazon EC2 instance so the export costs at most 10 lab credits a month and the worker at most 100. In this lab, Lambda charges 1 lab credit per million requests plus 0.0001 lab credits per GB-second, each second of run time times its GB of memory, and the instance costs a flat 50 lab credits a month, busy or idle. Every figure here and in the settings is a lab value.

params.label: Menu export: 30,000 requests a month, 800 ms, 512 MB
Order worker: 20 million requests a month, 150 ms, 1,024 MB

goals.label: The weekly menu export costs at most 10 lab credits a month
goals.hint: The export runs in one short burst a week and sits idle the rest of the month, so a flat monthly price pays mostly for hours when none of its code runs.

goals.label: The order queue worker costs at most 100 lab credits a month
goals.hint: The worker is never idle, so a charge for every request and every millisecond of run time keeps growing with the work until it passes a flat monthly price.

lines: The weekly export is idle almost all month, and Lambda charges only while its code runs, so the export costs about 1.23 lab credits on Lambda against the instance's flat 50.

The order worker is never idle, so Lambda's charges for its requests and run time reach 320 lab credits, and the always-on instance wins at a flat 50 because the worker leaves it no idle hours to pay for.
Allocated memory sets the price of each millisecond, so each second of the worker's 1,024 MB costs twice a second of the export's 512 MB.

options.why: Memory sets the speed and price of each run, but a function with no event source still never runs.

options.text: A function blueprint
options.why: A blueprint is a ready-made template for writing a function, not the event that starts the uploaded one.

steps.takeaway: With Lambda, AWS runs the environment, but the cafe still owns its code and the IAM permissions the function uses.

read.text: You own the code and the IAM roles and permissions the function uses to reach other services.

steps.stem: The ticket function now runs for each order, but every run fails with an access error when it reads order data held in another AWS service. Under the shared responsibility model, who fixes this, and where?

options.text: The cafe, in the function's IAM role
options.why: The cafe owns the IAM roles and permissions its function uses to reach other services, so the fix is the cafe's.

options.text: The cafe, in the function's memory setting
options.why: Memory sets the speed and price of each run; it grants no access, so a bigger setting leaves the error in place.

options.text: AWS, in the function's runtime environment
options.why: AWS patches and secures the environment the code runs in, but it does not grant the function access to the cafe's data.

options.text: AWS, in the servers the function runs on
options.why: AWS manages and allocates the underlying servers, while the permissions a function carries stay with the cafe.

steps.takeaway: In Lambda, memory sets both performance and the price of each millisecond, so a larger setting costs more per unit of run time.

read.text: You pay per millisecond of compute, priced by memory.

steps.stem: Tickets now print, but each one takes too long during the morning rush. The developer plans to give the function more memory. How does that change what the cafe pays?

options.text: Each millisecond of run time costs more
options.why: Lambda prices each millisecond by the memory allocated, so more memory raises the cost of each moment of run time.

options.text: The idle hours overnight start to be billed
options.why: Lambda bills only for compute time while code runs, so quiet hours with no orders still cost nothing.

options.text: A flat monthly fee replaces per-use billing
options.why: Raising memory does not change the billing model; Lambda still charges per millisecond of compute.

options.text: The bill stays the same as it was before
options.why: Memory is part of the price of each millisecond, so a larger setting does change the bill.

incidents.title: The patch nobody applied
incidents.brief: The cafe's ordering site went down after an old security hole on its EC2 servers was used against it, though a fix had been out for weeks. The owner now wants to know who owns which jobs, and whether to hand more of them to AWS.

steps.takeaway: On EC2, the operating system of each instance is the customer's to patch, while AWS covers the physical layer.

read.text: Unmanaged, like EC2: AWS covers the physical layer, while each instance's OS, network setup and apps are yours to set up, secure and maintain.

steps.stem: The fix that went unapplied was an update to the operating system on the cafe's EC2 instances. Under the shared responsibility model, who should have applied it?

options.text: The cafe, which owns each instance's OS
options.why: The update was to the instance's OS, which on unmanaged EC2 is the cafe's to set up, secure and maintain.

options.text: AWS, which owns each instance's OS
options.why: AWS does not own the OS on an EC2 instance; on an unmanaged service that layer sits with the customer.

options.text: The cafe, which owns the physical hosts
options.why: The physical hosts under EC2 are AWS's, and the missed fix was in the OS, not in the hosts.

options.text: AWS, which owns the physical hosts
options.why: AWS does own the physical hosts, but the missed fix was in the OS, which is the cafe's layer on EC2.

steps.takeaway: A managed service is configured once, and then AWS keeps it running with no server work for the customer.

read.text: After you configure one, AWS keeps it running with no server management on your part.

steps.stem: To cut upkeep, the owner moves the site's order queue from software on EC2 to Amazon SQS, a managed service. Which statement describes how the work on the queue is split after the move?

options.text: The cafe configures it, and AWS keeps it running
options.why: SQS is a managed service, so once the cafe configures the queue, AWS keeps it running with no server management on the cafe's part.

options.text: The cafe configures it and also keeps it running
options.why: That was the old setup with queue software on EC2; after the move to SQS, AWS keeps the queue running.

options.text: AWS runs the hardware, and the cafe runs the rest
options.why: That split fits unmanaged EC2, where AWS covers only the physical layer, not a managed queue like SQS.

options.text: AWS configures it, and the cafe keeps it running
options.why: The cafe still configures a managed service, and it is AWS, not the cafe, that keeps the queue running afterward.

steps.takeaway: Moving from EC2 to Lambda hands scaling to AWS, while the code and its security stay with the cafe.

read.text: You get fine control, but patching, scaling and the OS are yours while AWS runs the hardware.

steps.stem: The owner then moves the order-checking logic from EC2 to AWS Lambda, a fully managed service. Which job that was the cafe's on EC2 does AWS take over?

options.text: Keeping the function's code secure
options.why: Under Lambda, the application code and keeping it secure still stay with the cafe, so this job does not move.

options.text: Adding capacity for the lunch rush
options.why: Scaling was the cafe's job on EC2, and under a fully managed service like Lambda, AWS covers scaling instead.

options.text: Powering the data center's hardware
options.why: AWS already ran the hardware under the cafe's EC2 servers, so this job was never the cafe's to hand over.

options.text: Deciding which rules the code checks
options.why: The checking rules live in the cafe's application code, which stays with the cafe under Lambda.

incidents.title: A loyalty launch that slipped
incidents.brief: The chain's new loyalty programme launched a week late because the developer set up all of its hosting by hand. Before the next phase, the IT lead wants the right AWS compute service for each remaining piece.

steps.takeaway: Elastic Beanstalk turns code and settings into a scaled, load-balanced environment, work that raw EC2 leaves to the developer.

read.text: Give this fully managed service code and settings, and it builds the EC2 setup, scaling, load balancing and health checks.

steps.stem: For the loyalty site's next release, the developer moves from hand-built EC2 instances to AWS Elastic Beanstalk. Which work does Elastic Beanstalk take off the developer's hands?

options.text: Setting up load balancing and scaling
options.why: Given the code and settings, Elastic Beanstalk builds the EC2 setup, scaling, load balancing and health checks itself.

options.text: Scheduling batch jobs across a fleet
options.why: That is AWS Batch's work for heavy parallel jobs; Elastic Beanstalk runs the loyalty site as a web environment instead.

options.text: Running code only when an event arrives
options.why: That describes AWS Lambda's on-demand functions; Elastic Beanstalk keeps the loyalty site running on EC2 instances.

options.text: Orchestrating containers on Kubernetes
options.why: That is what Amazon EKS manages; Elastic Beanstalk builds an EC2 environment for the site rather than a Kubernetes cluster.

steps.takeaway: For a small, low-traffic site or a test site at a predictable monthly price, Lightsail is the simple pick.

read.text: A cost-effective bundle: virtual private servers (VPSs) plus storage, databases and networking, for a predictable monthly price.

steps.stem: One franchise wants a small, low-traffic site where it can test the loyalty pages before they go live. It wants a predictable monthly bill and a setup simpler than traditional hosting. Which service fits?

options.text: Amazon Lightsail
options.why: Lightsail bundles a virtual private server with storage and networking for a predictable monthly price, suited to dev and test.

options.text: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
options.why: Elastic Beanstalk builds a scaled EC2 environment and bills for those resources, more than a small test site calls for.

options.text: AWS Batch
options.why: AWS Batch schedules large compute jobs across a fleet; it does not host a small website.

options.text: AWS Outposts
options.why: Outposts brings AWS racks into a data center, far more than a small test site calls for.

steps.takeaway: When AWS compute must run in a company's own data center beside systems that cannot move yet, Outposts is the fit.

read.text: A fully managed hybrid cloud offering that brings AWS compute, storage and networking into your data center.

steps.stem: The loyalty system must work with an old till system in the chain's own data center, which cannot move yet. The IT lead wants AWS compute running right beside it, managed with the same tools and APIs as in the cloud. Which service fits?

options.text: AWS Outposts
options.why: Outposts brings AWS compute, storage and networking into the chain's own data center, run with the same tools and APIs.

options.text: Amazon Lightsail
options.why: Lightsail hosts small sites from AWS, not inside the chain's own data center beside the tills.

options.text: AWS Batch
options.why: AWS Batch schedules large compute jobs on a fleet in AWS and does not place any hardware on premises.

options.text: AWS Elastic Beanstalk
options.why: Elastic Beanstalk deploys web apps onto EC2 in AWS, not onto hardware in the chain's own building.
